headings.title: From a captured target to concrete resource identity
Deterministic scheduling profiles and resource locks
Scheduling preferences and exact user contracts

html:
Scheduling and concurrency

An activity is one admitted piece of work in a run. A batch groups proposed activities; a dependency graph determines readiness; resource admission decides whether ready work may overlap on the selected target. These layers remain distinct from durable background jobs and from the model's task board.

For graph acceptance, branch execution and input/recovery sequences, see Activity dependencies.

Settings → Resource locking owns participation in resource admission. The current product policy defaults to ON, with a wildcard that enables new tool families too. Saved policies retain their explicit choices: a family map without the wildcard does not enable an unlisted family. Missing policy data resolves through the current product defaults. Only master_enabled AND family_enabled participates: disabled families neither wait on nor impose resource conflicts, fairness queues, or inferred CPU, disk, GPU, network, lightweight and unknown-workload budgets. Worker limits, explicit dependencies, permissions, cancellation, duplicate-execution protection and database synchronization remain effective. Operating-system and application-native locking is unchanged.

Limit concurrent model calls is independent of the tool-locking master switch. Its default is on, with one active call per endpoint; turning tool locking off does not turn model capacity off. The saved model-family switch can disable that limit. The policy model and resolution functions own these defaults; Gateway policy reads validate the same policy model. The browser's policy-panel ownership describes revision conflicts and refresh behavior.

This is one persisted global policy, independent of conversation/run settings and Agent Checks. Canonical capability ownership assigns families; internal adapters retain their originating family. GET and PUT /api/agent/resource-locking expose the catalog, revision and Gateway synchronization status; saves require an expected revision. Authenticated Gateway updates are monotonic and durable. An older Gateway must be upgraded before execution; a disconnected Gateway remains pending synchronization.

Changes affect running and queued tasks. Disabling wakes resource waiters and resumes proven unstarted candidates through existing continuation fences. It never turns an uncertain execution into a completed receipt or automatically replays it. Enabling uses retained descriptions from active operations to gate new conflicts; already-running operations continue. The conflict and inferred-budget rules below apply only between participating families.

native/activities.py constructs and preflights batches, isolates activity state, joins workers and records results. native/dependency_graph.py validates predecessor edges and handles branch transitions. Branch-local behavior allows unrelated work to progress when the selected policy permits it; a failed or unresolved predecessor does not become a successful result. native/resource_scheduler.py maintains admission queues, classes, per-target capacity and claim lifetimes in the native store.

Captured multi-Gateway runs use these same owners. shell.parallel batches independent observations; schedule_activities expresses per-Gateway inspect/update/verify chains with target and depends_on. Concrete disjoint resources on different Gateways or on the same target may overlap within the applicable parallel and capacity limits. Overlapping concrete writes still serialize. Opaque effects remain disclosed uncertainty, and target selection alone is not proof that hidden external effects are independent.

Group receipts include each child's target/state and a bounded per-target outcome summary. Failures block dependent branches under the selected policy; unrelated targets continue. Unknown-effect guards can block overlapping work or wider progression within the same run according to the accepted branch policy; this is separate from physical resource locks. Saturated/offline targets do not reserve other Gateways' tokens.

The effective foreground upper bound comes from parallel_policy.execution_limit. When Parallel Execution is OFF it returns 1. Dependency admission can lower the limit and resource admission can delay work; neither can increase that bound. Turning OFF parallel execution therefore retains a single execution lane even when later scheduling features are enabled. Unknown resource classification has its own conservative capacity; it is not proof that work is read-only or safe to overlap.

Capacity policy resolution starts with product defaults, then global, conversation and explicit prompt settings. Runs retain accepted snapshots; missing legacy snapshots preserve disabled behavior. Capacity-policy revisions synchronize from persisted run policy. Resource locking participation always reads the current global policy. Use supported settings/override APIs for live changes; modifying an old global default does not mean every paused run inherits it. Cancellation generations, retained jobs and recovery records govern whether an activity can restart or release its claim.

The execution visualization reads activity/trace projections. It cannot admit work, release resource claims or declare dependency success. Inspect an activity's reason and receipt when diagnosing a wait; a queued state may represent dependency readiness, resource contention or another policy boundary.

Source owners: native/activities.py, dependency_graph.py, parallel_policy.py, dependency_policy.py, resource_policy.py, resource_scheduler.py.

When changing dispatch, keep budget spend, approval consumption, physical claims and receipts in their existing order in native/operations.py. Eligibility checks are not necessarily pure: some save state or record guard observations. The foreground invocation owns its cancellation watcher and signals completion before joining it. A projection refactor must not add an observer, polling tail or second job launch. The state publication contract also preserves the same Activity objects across saves while these workers are waiting.

Scheduling ownership and data flow

Scheduling answers three separate questions: which declared Activity is ready, whether it can reserve capacity and concrete resources, and whether the underlying execution has ended. The following map keeps those decisions with their existing owners. It also shows why a task waiting for capacity need not block independent work on another target.

flowchart TD Calls[Accepted calls and dependency edges] --> Ready[Activity or graph readiness] Ready --> Profile[Accepted scheduling profile] Evidence[Structural tool evidence and captured target] --> Profile Hints[Validated scheduling hints or exact contract] --> Profile Profile --> Queue[Pending queue and prospective access rows] Queue --> Admit[Atomic resource admission] Policy[Current family participation and accepted capacity policy] --> Admit Holds[Active and orphaned physical claims] --> Admit Admit -->|Blocked| Wait[Retain reason and wait for invalidation] Wait --> Ready Admit -->|Accepted| Execute[Normal claim, permission checks and execution] Execute --> Facts[Exact receipt or owned job observation] Facts --> Settle[Physical settlement] Settle -->|Execution still unresolved| Holds Settle -->|Release established| Wake[Publish released claims and wake waiters] Wake --> Ready Queue -. query only .-> View[Bounded admission and wait diagnostics] Holds -. query only .-> View

resource_scheduler.py coordinates profile attachment, admission, wait timing, recovery and diagnostics. Scheduler(store) selects MemoryScheduler for the application RAM authority; standalone stores use the SQL implementation. Neither backend calls a model to classify, choose or release work. Model-call leases are described separately in model decisions and capacity.

An accepted profile freezes operation identity, target, inferred/requested evidence and its digest. The latest resource-locking participation policy still determines which families impose conflicts and inferred demand. Explicit task dependencies, permissions, run/target/ global ceilings and duplicate-execution fences retain their own authority.

From a captured target to concrete resource identity

The Controller captures a pinned routing identity before acceptance and rechecks it in the admission transaction. Optional operator topology can merge known aliases; a missing physical enrollment does not create a global fallback lock. A routing target alone reserves no machine.

flowchart TD Context[Captured execution context] --> Identity{Current Controller or pinned Gateway?} Identity -->|No| Reject[Reject admission: requires_target_identity] Identity -->|Yes| Domain[Controller or pinned Gateway domain] Aliases[Optional verified physical alias evidence] --> Domain Domain --> Local[Scope concrete filesystem, repository, service and device keys] Endpoints[Named HTTP origins and explicit shared keys] --> Shared[Retain cross-target resource identity] Opaque[Opaque or incomplete effect evidence] --> Unknown[Disclose unresolved effects without fallback lock] Local --> Profile[Digest-covered namespace in accepted profile] Shared --> Profile Unknown --> Profile Transfer[Transfer source and destination] --> Both[Capture and charge each endpoint] Both --> Profile Profile --> Recheck[Revalidate trust and applicable topology during admission]

target_identity.py owns offline physical enrollment and the conversation/transfer binding boundary. execution_namespace.py normalizes concrete keys and validates captured trust. Local filesystem claims can include real-path and hard-link evidence from the extractor; remote claims use the normalized target path. Named HTTP resources are scoped to canonical origins, rather than treating URL paths as independent servers. The shared resources.py vocabulary handles subtree overlap and excludes host/global fallback fences.

Unknown effects are a disclosed limitation, not a proof of independence. Exact-effect replay and dependency guards remain separate: for example, disabling branch-local handling of unknown effects can block further affected work within a run without creating a global physical lock.

Atomic admission and fairness

Pending queue rows describe a request; they hold no active resource reservation. Admission publishes all relevant capacity and lock ownership together. A failed check can update its wait diagnosis but cannot leave partial tokens behind.

sequenceDiagram participant A as Ready Activity participant S as Scheduler participant T as RAM transaction or SQL writer participant E as Normal execution owner A->>S: Synchronize policy and attach accepted profile S->>T: Enqueue operation and prospective access rows together T-->>S: Existing accepted identity or committed pending row A->>S: Attempt acquisition S->>T: Check control fences and retained queue state T->>T: Validate captured target and applicable topology T->>T: Evaluate concrete conflicts and every capacity ceiling alt Conflict, capacity, target or orphan blocks progress T->>T: Retain correlated wait diagnosis T-->>S: Not admitted, no partial reservation S-->>A: Wait for an existing scheduler invalidation else Otherwise eligible T->>T: Compare eligible participants using aging and fairness alt Another eligible candidate ranks first T-->>S: Fairness wait with no active claims S-->>A: Remain queued else This candidate wins T->>T: Activate queue and locks, record admission and fairness time T-->>S: Commit complete ownership transition S-->>A: Admitted and notify after publication A->>E: Continue through ordinary authorization and execution end end

Concrete WRITE/READ and WRITE/WRITE overlaps serialize participating work; READ/READ can overlap. Observation controls use a separate admission lane. Physical aliases share their capacity domain and the most restrictive applicable override; transfers charge both captured endpoints. An admitted reservation is still not proof that a remote process has started.

After five seconds in the queue, aging gives queue time precedence over incoming unaged work. Otherwise ranking uses the configured effective priority, then the run's last admission, queue time and stable identities. Selection skips candidates that are blocked by current constraints. A disabled family does not join the resource fairness contest, but still obeys its applicable ordinary execution and total-capacity limits.

In RAM, the native repository's queue-change hook updates associated lock state in the same transaction. The standalone SQL schema in resource_locks.py uses queue triggers for that coupling. Diagnostic reads reuse admission calculations without invoking repair or changing ownership.

Receipt evidence and physical release

A task status, a worker returning, and a managed process ending are different facts. The settlement owner evaluates evidence for the exact run and operation. An owned job observation supersedes its older launch acknowledgement; a model-facing result projection cannot release another operation's claim.

flowchart TD Request[Receipt publication, job observation or owner settlement request] --> Queue{Claim already released?} Queue -->|Yes| Outcome[May resolve later outcome without reopening ownership] Queue -->|No| Evidence[Read exact owned job and correlated receipt evidence] Evidence --> Ended{Lifecycle proves execution inactive?} Ended -->|Yes| Release[Publish done queue, released locks and settlement event] Ended -->|No| Local{Eligible local control return with no external lifecycle?} Local -->|Yes| Release Local -->|No| Hold[Keep claim or mark reconciliation required] Release --> Wake[Wake affected waiters after publication] Hold --> Observe[Existing lifecycle owner observes same execution] Observe --> Evidence

operation_settlement.py retains unknown history even when physical inactivity allows capacity release. A live managed job, an uncertain dispatched operation or a mismatched observation cannot be cleared by a local worker's return. Authenticated foreground inspection can settle the matching orphan; managed jobs first pass through their monotone observation writer. Sequence parents additionally require dispatcher closure and valid evidence for every claimed child.

A retained HTTP or unsafe-action input continuation has a narrow reopening exception: positive no-start evidence, the current progression lease and a not-yet-consumed continuation generation. Its earlier no-start receipt cannot release the later physical attempt. Completed or uncertain execution otherwise needs a new authorized identity, not a repeated acquisition of the old one.

Recovery and observation boundaries

Recovery reconstructs scheduling facts from saved evidence. It does not restart a command to learn whether the previous command finished. RAM startup performs its reconciliation scan before the store becomes ready; normal live RAM admission does not repeat that history scan.

sequenceDiagram participant B as Exclusive Controller bootstrap participant M as MemoryScheduler participant S as Native RAM authority participant P as Physical settlement owner participant O as Later observation or run owner B->>M: Recover retained queue before readiness M->>S: Close never-admitted pending entries M->>S: Mark prior active ownership orphaned M->>P: Reconcile retained exact evidence P->>S: Release proven inactive claims and retain unresolved claims B->>S: Complete bootstrap and publish readiness O->>M: Read bounded status or admission diagnosis M-->>O: Coherent facts without probes or claim mutation alt Existing lifecycle owner obtains correlated new evidence O->>P: Publish exact receipt or owned job observation P->>S: Settle queue and lock state together S-->>O: Notify affected waiters after publication else Evidence remains unavailable O->>S: Preserve physical ownership and recovery requirement end

The standalone SQL backend performs owner/job reconciliation in its admission transaction. A dead local owner can discard an unstarted pending reservation; uncertain active work becomes orphaned. Both backends preserve accepted profiles and require release evidence for physical work. Jobs, waits and resume describes subsequent observation, continuation scheduling and human-input precedence.

Execution data and runtime services

execution/context.py owns the target snapshot boundary. target_snapshot copies explicit routing, platform, capability, directory and credential-reference fields. It recursively detaches plain data and rejects live objects within those fields. target_snapshots applies the same boundary to a selected-target map. Only transient planning may include the authenticated preflight profile; saved targets omit current dispatch IDs, timeout overrides and preflight state.

RuntimeHost and the execution engine own clients, management services, stores, connections and cancellation controls. Tool contexts borrow these objects; they are not durable records. bind_target replaces target data while retaining the current runtime's service references. It does not copy services or inherit omitted machine defaults from another Gateway. Gateway selection remains run-wide authority.

Background registration, job launch persistence, foreground supervision, external blocker recovery, dependency activities and artifact collection use this boundary. Initial preflight copies target data rather than the entire tool context. Activity routing and run restoration use the same target projection. A new gateway_* field does not become persistent or machine-local merely because of its name.

OAuth callbacks use the same projection to detach routes while borrowing live services. Gateway transfers use the shared activity target binding and save explicit ID/path checkpoints. Scheduled events and monitors already capture explicit admission scope; queued-task compilation and continuations copy saved data. These paths do not clone a live runtime. The Gateway ingress prefix filter remains a rejection boundary for untrusted routing fields, not a rule for copying or persisting context.

An invalid snapshot raises the source-owned execution_context_not_data runtime fault. Existing fault handling stops inference and retains the diagnostic rather than asking the model to retry the command. Target process failures retain their ordinary execution semantics.

Human interaction checkpoints

Authority waits are runtime controls. When a future-work request needs the disabled Schedules capability, discovery immediately opens one approval card and stops inference. The temporal tool filter needs no special ask_user exception. Allow renews capability authority in a child continuation while preserving the captured due time and future task. Permission Policy can still require a separate approval for schedule.create. Deny creates no schedule and resumes with a durable denial fact. Repository inspection, staging, commits and pushes belonging to the future task do not run during this wait.

native/authority_control.py keeps independent Activity approvals addressed by their Activity and operation identities. Accepted replies use the existing durable Activity wake journal; they cannot overwrite another running Activity or answer its checkpoint.

ask_user is a conversation control, independent of Background Activities and Resource Scheduling settings. Standalone calls go directly to native control dispatch. Explicit schedule_activities graphs may still contain ask_user nodes; unresolved nodes block dependents and parent inference. Already-started jobs continue under their existing identities and resource claims. Independent, already-declared DAG branches remain eligible for admission; their Activity-local running state cannot clear the parent's question or reply identity. Manual Pause and Stop still prevent admission. No new model decisions occur until the human checkpoint resolves.

At wait and completion boundaries, an actionable human wait takes precedence over waiting_job. The shared Activity projection maps ordinary input, credential and approval waits to their existing dedicated parent states. Older checkpoints with a local ordinary wait and a running/job-waiting parent are repaired before inference. Multiple ordinary waits surface in accepted batch/Activity order, with persisted record order as the fallback for legacy checkpoints. Answering one exposes the next unresolved wait without a model polling call. Agent Checks shows the selected ordinary Activity as waiting for a reply in the conversation; its duplicate text form is suppressed.

An explicit graph that reaches clarification before concrete work leaves terminal output intent unfrozen. Its accepted proposal is retained on concrete Activities and frozen when such work starts. Existing frozen output contracts remain unchanged by clarification.

Structural resource admission

The model represents independent work as separate calls or shell.parallel; smTO alone decides which Activities can overlap. Use shell.sequence for known ordered steps, side-effect dependencies and fail-fast ordering. Sequence steps have separate subprocesses and explicit working directories; shared shell state requires one ordinary Shell command. The runtime never rewrites semicolons into background processes or adds a planning call.

Resource classification reuses shell_operation_facts and the effect system's read proof. Punctuation is not a resource class: echo start; du /tmp; echo done and du /cache/* | sort -rh | head -25 claim disk_read_heavy=1. File output and mutating find forms retain conservative disk/unknown admission. Unsupported substitutions, external scripts and unknown components retain an unknown demand.

Immutable ResourceClaims holds bounded integer tokens for every required dimension. Pipelines union dimensions; sequential commands and Shell Sequence steps hold the maximum per dimension for their Activity lifetime. Tokens count Activities, not child processes. Incidental lightweight components add no token when substantive work exists. A CPU/network Activity reserves both dimensions atomically with global, run and Gateway slots; waiting work never holds a partial reservation. Selection can skip a full class or target.

Policy-model defaults and fresh-installation presets are distinct. A new settings store seeds global values from installation_defaults.py; an existing store keeps its saved choices. Removing a global override can expose the policy-model defaults again. Accepted snapshots retain their own limits.

Capacity or mode Policy-model default Fresh-installation global preset
P1 foreground 8 16
P4 resource mode Auto Custom
P4 Activities per run 8 8
Activities per Gateway 8 8
Disk read-heavy per Gateway 2 16
Disk-heavy / unknown per Gateway 1 / 1 16 / 8
CPU / network / GPU / lightweight per Gateway 2 / 2 / 1 / 8 16 / 16 / 16 / 8

Global Activity slots have a separate default of 32. The ParallelPolicy and ResourcePolicy models own the first column. A higher resource-class limit cannot exceed the applicable total, run, target or global ceiling.

Settings → Scheduler capacity collects the global parallel, background and dependency activity ceilings, graph sizes, resource budgets, fairness, global Activity slots and per-Gateway overrides. The section has its own navigation link and searchable field labels. Enable the corresponding features in Asynchronous task execution; inactive features keep their capacity controls disabled. Choose Custom to edit CPU, disk read-heavy, disk-heavy, network, GPU, lightweight and unknown budgets. Policy controls save on change. These inferred budgets apply only to families enabled in Resource locking; general activity limits remain independently effective.

Control Allowed values

Scheduled activities per run 1–16

Under Gateway overrides, choose a Gateway, edit its limits and select Save capacity. These are the same shared limits exposed by Gateway Management → Details → Activity capacity. Clearing a Gateway override restores Auto without changing the global policy. Global policy defaults apply to newly accepted tasks; shared Gateway overrides and global Activity slots apply to subsequent admissions across tasks. Lowering a limit does not cancel running work.

Agent Checks → Advanced resource limits continues to support conversation, prompt and run Custom values. An override never exceeds the P1, run, global or target-total ceilings. Auto is static and conservative; no hardware benchmark or natural-language capacity estimate is used. The policy-model defaults permit seven compatible lightweight observations to overlap when the other applicable gates allow it, with P4 enabled or disabled. That is a capacity example, not a promise of measured concurrency. Disk, CPU, network, GPU and unknown budgets remain separate constraints. Explicit lower run, Gateway and global ceilings remain authoritative.

Queue records retain sparse capacity claims beside the display class. The default Server keeps these in RAM; standalone and recovery SQL encode the claims as JSON. Legacy mixed maps to the unknown bucket. ResourcePolicy.from_snapshot restores historical P4 run/Gateway/lightweight fallbacks of six/three/four, preserves explicit saved values and uses serialize when the mutation policy is absent. Other missing fields use the model schema defaults. Missing or empty historical policy remains disabled. Existing P1 foreground snapshots are resolved by their separate policy owner.

Policy resolution chooses one complete value in global, conversation, prompt order; it does not merge fields across those scopes. Saved global/conversation values use the historical snapshot rules, whereas an explicit prompt or product default uses the current policy model. bind restores a saved run before considering new-request defaults and places a detached snapshot in execution context. Neither resolution nor binding grants execution permission. See resource_policy.py.

Availability updates merge only their supplied signal fields, preserving saturation. Other scheduler configuration keys replace their stored value. Policy snapshots, job reconciliation, receipt identity and Stop retain their separate ownership.

Activity details show claims and the admission snapshot: P1 ceiling, run/global/Gateway usage and limits, each claimed dimension, policy source, Gateway overrides, and the actual limiting factor. Compact labels distinguish disk-read capacity from Gateway-total waits. These diagnostics describe admission time; they do not claim to be live hardware telemetry. Classification, capacity release and ready dispatch use zero LLM calls.

NVIDIA inspection effects

Shell effects use literal executable/argv evidence through execution/shell_operations.py. Its execution/nvidia_smi.py helper proves bounded NVIDIA summary, GPU-list, diagnostic and selective CSV query forms, including GPU selectors. For example, nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,power.limit,power.draw --format=csv is read-only. Known configuration operations such as -pl 250, -pm 1 and --gpu-reset are effectful (gpu_configuration). Unsupported options, mixed operations, malformed arguments and NVIDIA continuous-monitoring modes remain unknown.

Existing Shell redirects, compounds, wrapper restrictions and authorization still apply. Activity descriptors receive these same facts; no user command whitelist or model classification call is involved. Bounded local NVIDIA queries claim lightweight capacity and a GPU read lock; configuration claims GPU capacity and a GPU write lock. A query cannot race a conflicting configuration operation. The exact supported grammar and verification are recorded in docs/nvidia-smi-effect-classification-report.md.

The first-class GPU skill distinguishes lightweight telemetry from gpu_heavy configuration. Its Gateway job claims exact UUID resources and refuses unknown-effect replay. The configured GPU capacity remains authoritative; it does not prevent unrelated telemetry.

Literal remote inspections

Bounded ssh host 'literal program' and sshpass -p VALUE ssh ... / sshpass -e ssh ... forms propagate the remote program's canonical effect, including NVIDIA configuration mutations and unknown commands. The accepted transport options include separate -p and -l operands, -T, -n, -4, -6, -q, -v/-vv/-vvv, and explicit bounded -o StrictHostKeyChecking=..., UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null, ConnectTimeout=... values. Forwarding, proxies, local commands, persistent controls and other unsupported options cannot inherit a read proof. Recursion stops after four SSH layers.

A proven read whose literal SSH chain ends in one supported nvidia-smi --query-gpu=... CSV query claims lightweight=1 on the dispatching Gateway. The remote GPU is not that Gateway's local GPU resource. Other remote reads, including du /, find / and large content reads, retain unknown=1; a read proof alone does not imply lightweight demand. The Activity target remains the dispatching smTO Gateway, distinct from the SSH destination. Foreground, resource, global and Gateway limits and accepted policy snapshots remain authoritative; Parallel OFF still executes sequentially. New product defaults permit seven such probes on one dispatching Gateway without registering their SSH destinations as smTO Gateways. The complete grammar and verification are recorded in docs/nested-ssh-effect-propagation-report.md; seven-host capacity acceptance is recorded in docs/safe-parallel-wave-expansion-report.md.

Timing summaries use recorded physical execution intervals, not the parallel tool name or configured ceiling. The same seven-item batch can truthfully display Ran up to 7 simultaneously, Ran up to 2 simultaneously, or Ran sequentially, depending on observed overlap. Classification, waves, admission, waiting and joining add no inference.

When one model decision contains ordinary tools and run waits, the runtime executes the ordinary tools first under the existing concurrency and authorization policy. It then dispatches wait_for_event, manage_job(action="wait"), wait_for_activity, wait_for_any_activity, and wait_for_all_required_activities against the parent run in their original relative order. Each wait settles before the next registers. Relative delays begin at registration; absolute deadlines stay unchanged. An explicit background launch completes its ordinary call when the launch receipt returns; job or Activity waits govern the process lifetime. Waits remain prohibited inside dependency-graph nodes.

The accepted batch persists deferred calls and progress before execution. Parent wait registration saves its identity with the pending wait and continuation note, so restart can recover the same timer without replaying ordinary effects or asking the model to correct its decision. Failed, denied, cancelled, or uncertain siblings skip the deferred waits with correlated results naming the failed operations. A registration failure skips later waits. Approval and input suspend progression, Pause preserves it, and Stop closes unregistered calls. Completion cannot pass outstanding accepted waits. Trace events wait.deferred, wait.registered, and wait.skipped describe these transitions; UI wait status and countdown continue to use the parent's actual pending wait.

Top-level tasks

The composer’s Depends on selector creates an explicit success edge to the chosen live task in the same conversation. It defaults to No dependency — run independently for each submission and resets on conversation changes. This graph is owned by tasks/dependencies.py, separately from the native Activity graph described above.

Task creation validates and saves the exact selected task ID in the task repository's atomic transaction. The default Server publishes to its RAM state hub; standalone SQL stores use a SQLite writer transaction. See MemoryTaskStore.create_task and MemoryDependencies. Running and queued tasks are selectable; a selected task remains selected even if it finishes before submission. Legacy API clients can still request the immediately previous task. Queue reordering changes only queue order. The existing conversation coordinator scans for the oldest runnable task, skipping waiting or failed dependency branches. Parallel Agent tasks retain global capacity and accepted policy limits; Conversation/Ask tasks retain their exclusive shared transcript gate.

Failure and interruption affect explicit dependents, not the entire conversation queue. Retry retains the logical task ID, allowing descendants to resume eligibility automatically after success. Cancellation of a dependent remains explicit and final until a user intentionally reopens that task. Native permission, resource and reconciliation rules continue to apply when eligible work executes.

Running task cards offer Pause beside Stop on desktop and mobile, including tasks waiting for a job or event. Pause lets the current action finish, preserves progress and then offers Resume on the same task. Stop remains available while Pause is pending.

The control boundary has three distinct outcomes:

Action State and execution behavior
Pause Queues an intent. The current owner settles accepted results, validates message correlations, then saves the original wait and remaining wall budget. It does not cancel a job or answer a human checkpoint.
Resume Restores the saved destination and wall budget, or accepts explicit replacement limits. An unanswered human checkpoint remains waiting. A replaced or stopping run rejects the request.
Stop Publishes cancellation authority and rejects further decision acceptance before asynchronous transport/job cleanup. Already recorded receipts survive; a claimed operation without a result remains an unknown remote effect.

StopPolicy defaults to instant. graceful allows accepted work to settle for five seconds by default, with a configurable range of 0.1–300 seconds; an immediate Stop can escalate it. The policy is selected as a whole from prompt, conversation, global or default settings in that precedence order and snapshotted for the run. RAM continuation scheduling owns graceful deadlines. The standalone SQL path uses a bounded polling worker. Cleanup failure does not restore permission to run or prove that a remote operation was undone.

The implementation boundaries are pause.py, memory_pause.py, cancellation.py, memory_cancellation.py and stop_policy.py. RAM acceptance and disk recovery are separate, as explained in state and recovery.

Stopped and interrupted tasks offer Continue task and Restart task together on desktop and mobile. Continue preserves execution progress. Restart begins a fresh attempt from the saved user inputs, retaining the target, model, permissions and other task settings. It rebuilds execution progress and keeps previous results as historical context. Previous external actions are not undone, and unresolved effects still require reconciliation. Both actions retain the logical task ID and queue dependencies; repeated clicks on either action return the same child attempt.

Stalled, failed and paused tasks also offer Restart task, including tasks stopped by a context-window overflow. Resume, when available, keeps the current attempt; Restart clears its execution context and starts a new attempt. Restart becomes available after the previous execution settles and while the task still owns its conversation position. A replaced attempt cannot resume or launch another child. Restart retains the original model settings: after correcting a context or output limit in Settings, submit a new task to use that configuration.

Stalled task cards also offer Stop and, when a next queued task is eligible, Skip on desktop and mobile. Stop cancels the stalled attempt and lets the next task proceed. Skip releases the attempt's run slot while keeping its native status, results and history unchanged. Failed, stopped and interrupted cards can also Skip to the next task. Both actions save a decision against the observed request and waive only the selected next task's dependency on it; other prerequisites still apply. Later chained tasks wait for their own predecessor. The observed queue version and next task ID reject stale or duplicate requests.

The saved queue decision prevents automatic execution of a skipped attempt and survives server recovery. The queue reconciler completes a saved Stop decision before dispatching its successor. Skip uses an interrupted task-ledger projection to release capacity while the native run remains stalled. Explicit Resume must reclaim an available slot; a skipped Conversation turn cannot resume after a later turn has taken ownership of the shared journal.

Task records retain optional edge arrays, immutable creation order and cached dependency projections. Legacy tasks can have no edges. Recovery derives dependency state from recovered execution outcomes; missing or corrupt dependency targets block execution. Task checkpoints record transitions, and the execution visualization keeps top-level edges distinct from internal activity dependencies.

Structured waits and independent branches

Dependency edges express required predecessor evidence; resource capacity expresses an admission constraint. Sharing a target, Shell capability or conversation creates no synthetic dependency. Ready candidates are scanned past blocked branches: an unrelated lightweight read can start while a disk read is held, and another Gateway remains eligible when the first Gateway is saturated. Real global/run ceilings, effect overlaps and failed or unresolved prerequisites still block the affected work. A task lane likewise skips an ineligible dependent row while preserving explicit dependency selection.

Retained admission waits distinguish dependency, effect guard, resource class, Gateway, run, global and fairness constraints. They preserve wait-start time and bounded blocker identities; foreign runs expose only aggregate blocker counts. Scheduler.observe reads these facts and the same admission diagnostic calculation without _reap, PID probing or state repair. Existing execution/lifecycle writers remain the only claim owners.

Deterministic barrier tests in tests/test_independent_work_hardening.py hold A, keep B pending on A, allow independent C (and E on another target), and prevent truly conflicting D until A releases. They also cover real ceiling limits, task-lane independence and bound inputs through the existing graph tests. Timing/order evidence is recorded in docs/assets/instant-refresh-hardening/scheduler-concurrency.json.

Deterministic scheduling profiles and resource locks

Scheduling has three different units of ownership:

Unit Owner Lifetime
Logical task and predecessor edges Task store / dependency graph Until the accepted task settles
Agent turn native/agent_turns.py Actual model call, including its physical I/O lifetime
Physical activity Existing P4 resource scheduler From atomic admission until physical release evidence

A task waiting for a job, approval, event, or resource is still open but does not own an Agent turn. Ready startup reservations prevent excess dispatch before the first model call. Actual calls acquire leases through AgentTurns: the default Server uses MemoryAgentTurns and atomic RAM admission; the standalone store uses SQLite. The configured Agent concurrency limit bounds calls across runs. Nested tracing uses the same lease. Cancellation of a caller cannot release a permit while its underlying model I/O remains active. Background jobs retain physical capacity and locks independently. Existing bounded executors still limit dispatch workers; parallel Agent journals do not use open-task count as a physical or model-capacity proxy. Shared Conversation/Ask journals retain their ordering rules.

Each activity receives an immutable SchedulingProfileV2: operation/target identity, execution mode and priority, multidimensional capacity, READ/WRITE/EXCLUSIVE/OBSERVE identities, effect and confidence, provenance, unresolved scope, requested and inferred evidence, and a SHA-256 digest. Background is an execution mode, not an unknown resource class. For example, a literal local download with an explicit output has network and disk-write demand and a destination write lock whether it runs foreground or background. An opaque program still has unresolved effects even when its CPU demand is known.

The shared structural Shell parser supplies bounded executable facts. Native Files, KV, GPU, and existing Docker contracts supply their established resource proofs. Local filesystem identities include lexical paths, real paths and existing hard-link identities; parent/child paths conflict. Remote filesystem claims name the normalized target path; unknown aliases are not replaced with a host or filesystem-root reservation. Namespace V2 binds each resource to its captured Gateway and pinned TLS enrollment. Physical topology merges known aliases of one host. Shared storage requires an explicit shared-resource key. The Controller has a separate local domain. Transfers claim their source and destination paths.

A host is a routing target, never a lock. Opaque Shell/Python programs retain any concrete inferred resources and disclose unresolved effects without a host/global fallback lock. The operator is responsible for scheduling workloads whose hidden effects could collide. Named HTTP origins and explicit shared resources still conflict across targets. Missing or changed target trust prevents dispatch with requires_target_identity.

READ/READ overlaps. WRITE/READ and WRITE/WRITE overlapping resources serialize. Exclusive assertions add conflicts; observing a managed job does not lock its workload. Capacity and locks activate together in the store's admission transaction. The default Server's MemoryScheduler publishes through the RAM hub; the standalone SQL scheduler uses BEGIN IMMEDIATE. Pending lock records describe prospective access but impose no active reservation. A pending candidate owns neither partial capacity nor active locks. RAM publication and disk recovery are separate boundaries, described in state and recovery. Admission examines compatible candidates beyond a blocked head. Persisted fairness and aging still apply.

All mutation policies enforce overlap on concrete resources. Disjoint resources on the same host can run concurrently. P4 OFF preserves P1/P2/P3 admission; turning it off does not discard concrete claims already owned by live work.

Per-target capacity uses the same captured host/Gateway domains, including both endpoints of a transfer. Proven aliases share limits and the most restrictive applicable override. An explicit Controller global_slots ceiling still applies; diagnostics call this waiting_capacity_global, not a resource lock.

Host locks, unbounded wildcard locks, and V1/global claim compatibility are removed. Restart does not synthesize historical global fences. Current concrete claims retain operation ownership until physical completion or reconciliation. Server and Gateway both use the shared resource overlap rules; both need this code update.

Resource inspection distinguishes local/shared lock waits, physical reconciliation, target availability, fairness and capacity dimensions. An admitted reservation alone does not prove a running process. Retained observer deadlines and liveness explain what happens next; foreign operation IDs and resource paths are omitted. The bounded /api/agent/resource-scheduling/waits/{request_id} read joins lock and accepted dependency edges without Gateway probes, model calls or ownership writes. Long silent execution is not a deadlock. Only a closed cycle with no independent progress proves deadlock; an uncertain physical owner remains a reconciliation problem. Diagnostics never release it.

Scheduling preferences and exact user contracts

Desktop and mobile Agent Checks expose optional scheduling preset, mode and priority. Shell/Python tool schemas expose __smto_scheduling hints. This reserved envelope is removed before business argument validation/execution. A hint may add capacity or exclusive access; it cannot erase a write, narrow unknown scope, grant permissions, or rewrite a tool's accepted lifecycle. Background preferences use existing captured Shell job support; foreground preferences suppress automatic promotion. Other tools preserve their supported execution modes.

An advanced user can GET /api/agent/resource-scheduling/profiles/{request_id}/{operation_id} and PUT the /contract subresource with expected_profile_digest and contract. Contracts bind the exact tool, target, canonical argument digest, cwd, and script/content SHA-256 when locally available. The operation must be pending and never admitted. The update compares the old digest and commits profile, queue demand, and pending locks in one transaction. Revisions must increase. Accepted execution mode cannot change through this endpoint; the profile is frozen at admission.

An exact contract may replace unresolved inferred demand with a user declaration while retaining known concrete reads, writes and substantive capacity. Its confidence is recorded as user_declared on revision. For example, an opaque downloader can declare network and disk capacity and fs:local:/models/output; the declaration applies to that invocation only. With Namespace V2, a revision must have one captured execution target, scopes added identities to it and retains existing namespace uncertainty. A multi-endpoint transfer cannot reshape its endpoint ownership through this one-target contract API.

For participating resource-locking families, dispatch rechecks a captured content digest before executing an exact contract. A changed script produces scheduling_contract_mismatch. This check is conditional on resource-locking participation; disabling that family bypasses this scheduling-specific recheck. Capability, permission, unsafe-action, target and approval checks retain their own ownership. A scheduling assertion does not authorize execution, and its strict schema rejects permission or approval fields.

Profile construction and revision owners

scheduling_profile.py builds the validated evidence. It hashes canonical sorted JSON for arguments and profile identity; created_at is excluded from the profile digest. Reloading a supplied inconsistent digest fails validation. Inline Python text has a content hash. Local Shell script hashing supports one literal invocation of a recognized interpreter and reads at most one MiB of a regular file; missing, unsupported, remote or oversized script inputs have no content hash. Neither classification nor hashing executes the program or calls a model.

flowchart LR A[Tool arguments and native contracts] --> B[Structural evidence and capacity] H[Optional hint or exact contract] --> C[Reconcile requested and inferred evidence] B --> C C --> P[Immutable profile with digest] P --> Q[Pending queue and prospective locks] Q --> T[Atomic admission] T --> X[Existing execution owner] U[User revision with expected digest] --> V[Pending and lifecycle checks] Q --> V V --> Q

A hint can add preset demand and priority. Its read-only preset cannot erase detected mutations or unresolved effects. Native observation uses separate lightweight demand and control priority. An exact contract must match its operation binding, declare nonempty capacity and omit observation identities. Construction preserves the tool's captured mode and records a reason when the requested mode differs.

For live edits, revise_contract creates a candidate profile. It does not verify queue or Stop state itself. The resource-scheduling routes and RAM policy writer own the transaction, pending-state and digest checks, captured-mode rejection and persistence. The RAM writer also checks cancellation and deletion in that same transaction. Success returns the revised profile, wakes admission and publishes a run invalidation without a model call. Missing queue/profile records return 404; stale or already-started edits return 409; mismatched bindings, unsupported mode changes and other invalid contracts return 422.

The GET profile response includes both profile and admission. Use the returned profile.profile_digest as expected_profile_digest; do not recompute it after editing a JSON copy. A second accepted contract must increase the previous contract revision. Failed validation leaves the accepted profile and demand unchanged.

Policy and shared-capacity API

The same route group exposes these distinct controls:

Route Scope and effect
GET /api/agent/resource-scheduling Effective policy, product defaults, global source and optional conversation override. An unknown requested conversation returns 404.
PUT /api/agent/resource-scheduling Global/conversation settings or a live-run policy. Null clears a settings override; for a run it restores the initial captured policy/source. An optional policy_revision compares the current run revision.
GET /api/agent/resource-scheduling/capacity Scheduler-owned capacity snapshot.
PUT /api/agent/resource-scheduling/capacity Controller global_slots (1–128, default 32 if omitted), plus optional observation_slots (1–16). This is not a partial patch of global_slots.
GET / PUT /api/agent/resource-scheduling/gateways/{target} Read or save the validated capacity override for the target key. This does not enroll or contact the Gateway.

Live-run policy writes reject terminal/cancelled state, increment the revision, and update both current and resume snapshots. A later owner checkpoint merges the separate accepted resource-policy revision. Global settings and observation-slot configuration are separate writes; setting both shared slot limits also performs separate writes. These routes do not promise a cross-store transaction. Capacity changes affect subsequent admissions and do not cancel work already running.

Observation, diagnostics and recovery

inspect_execution, saved context/result reads, job observation/control and native agent.info remain available independently of workload saturation. Controller reads use a bounded observation reservation (default four); control has a separate reservation. Nested observation shares its reservation. Status reads are query-only: they neither reap claims nor invoke a model. Managed job status uses existing job progress and liveness facts, without scheduling a generic Shell check behind the job itself.

Capacity snapshots contain compact activity counts, target usage, up to 32 waiter summaries, Agent-turn counts/metrics and observation capacity. They omit full arguments, receipts, traces and task history. Detailed profiles load by operation identity on demand. Activity details distinguish resource-lock waits from capacity, fairness and target waits, and expose inferred/requested/effective evidence. Physical intervals, capacity/lock waits, peak concurrency, critical-path estimates and aggregate Agent-turn timings remain separate.

In-process releases, model-turn completion, terminal job evidence, cancellation and policy changes invalidate scheduler waiters. Versioned condition waits avoid lost notifications; a 500 ms fallback covers cross-process updates and missed external events. Durable task queue dispatch also subscribes to invalidations. No 50 ms capacity polling is required.

Accepted profiles and normalized locks are stored with the queue. Supported legacy activity restoration uses conservative saved claims, without running new classifiers. Reloading accepted profiles validates their existing digest; it does not reinterpret the command using new hints.

In the default Server, MemoryScheduler.recover runs during exclusive bootstrap. It closes retained pending entries, marks previously active/orphaned entries as orphaned, and asks operation_settlement to reconcile all retained ownership before readiness. A later acquire on an orphaned entry waits for physical reconciliation. Live RAM admission never runs that recovery scan: _reap is a no-op, and receipt/job publication owns settlement. An active reservation can be reacquired idempotently; a released one cannot be reopened by another acquire.

Unknown physical activity retains its claim until evidence proves release. Logical cancellation, loss of connectivity or an unknown outcome alone does not prove death. Conversely, mechanically ended work can release capacity while its historical outcome stays unknown. A local owner return can settle an eligible control reservation with no external lifecycle; it cannot override an unresolved dispatched invocation or job. Queue changes and retained lock status/timestamps publish through the native repository's change hook in the same transaction. Deleting pending queue work marks its retained locks released rather than deleting history.

The RAM observer captures configuration, projected holders, retained wait evidence and settlement facts from one coherent view. It performs no Gateway probe, recovery pass or release. Wait records are keyed by run, operation and diagnostic kind: repeated updates replace their detail while preserving the first occurrence time. This bounds each kind's history and keeps its wait start stable; it is not an append-only chronology of every admission attempt.

All classification, scheduling, observation, stall checks and recovery are deterministic and add zero model calls. See docs/smart-effect-resource-scheduler-vnext-report.md for exact validation commands, benchmark scope and remaining conservative cases.
